initial_requirements: The Federal Highway Administration needs the Clarus system to collect, quality-control, and share environmental and road-condition observations from transportation networks. Transportation agencies, observation-system operators, weather-service providers, and researchers should be able to contribute or use the data. The system is intended to support safer road operations, timely responses to weather, and improved forecasting through an integrated source of surface transportation observations.

messages.content: Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the Clarus Weather System so we can clearly understand the needed scope and requirements. Before we begin, are you in line with the scope of this interview, or do your expectations differ?

Yes, I’m aligned with that scope. I’m here to help clarify what Clarus needs to do for collecting, quality-controlling, and sharing the transportation weather and road-condition observations, along with how different users and agencies will interact with it.
Thank you. To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m speaking as someone representing the stakeholder side for the Clarus effort, with a focus on how the system will support transportation operations and data sharing. My perspective is centered on the needs of FHWA and the agencies and partners who will contribute to and use the observations.
Thank you. Could you briefly describe the Clarus project in two to four sentences?

Clarus is intended to bring together environmental and road-condition observations from transportation networks into one integrated system. It will quality-control that data and make it available to transportation agencies, observation-system operators, weather-service providers, and researchers. The goal is to improve road safety, support faster weather response, and help with better forecasting.

Ok, now that I know the general goal, let’s talk a bit about the systems and workflows you currently use. Can you describe the current process or system you use for collecting, quality-controlling, and sharing these observations?

Right now, the data is typically collected through a mix of roadway sensors, station systems, and weather-related sources operated by different agencies or vendors, and each source often has its own process. Quality control is usually handled locally or in separate downstream workflows, so the checks and formats aren’t consistent across all sources. Sharing also tends to happen through different channels and interfaces, which makes it harder to combine the observations quickly and use them in a unified way.
Ok, what current processes do you want to change or improve, or what are the main features you hope to get from this project?

The main thing we want to improve is having one consistent pipeline for bringing in the observations, checking their quality, and distributing them in a usable form. We also want less manual reconciliation between sources, better standardization of the data, and more timely availability for operational users. On top of that, it would help if the system made it easier for researchers and weather providers to access the same trusted dataset without each group having to build separate integrations.
Based on your description, should Clarus also include role-based access or different data access methods for agencies, providers, and researchers?

Yes, I think that makes sense. Different users will likely need different access levels and different ways to retrieve the data, especially if some information is operationally sensitive or needs to be published in a controlled way. I’d expect agencies and operators to have broader access for contribution and monitoring, while researchers and weather providers may mainly need read access or standardized feeds, but I’d want to verify the exact rules with the program owners.
Are there any other features you would like to see in this project, perhaps something that has not been the primary focus so far?

It would be helpful if the system also provided good reporting and visibility into data quality, source status, and outages so users can trust what they’re seeing. I’d also like to see strong metadata and traceability, so people can understand where an observation came from and how it was processed. If possible, alerting for missing or suspect data would be valuable too.

Thank you. So far, I’ve captured these main features: a consistent ingestion pipeline, quality control, standardized distribution, reduced manual reconciliation, timely availability, role-based access, reporting/visibility into data quality and source status, metadata and traceability, and alerting for missing or suspect data. Is that an accurate summary?
Yes, that’s an accurate summary of what I’ve described. The only thing I’d add is that the access and distribution methods may need to vary by user type, but the overall list is right.
Which of these main features should be the highest priority for Clarus?

The highest priority should be the consistent ingestion, quality control, and standardized distribution pipeline. That’s the core of what Clarus needs to do, and the other features really support that foundation. After that, I’d put timely availability and traceability very high, since users need to trust and act on the data quickly.
Please elaborate on what you want the consistent ingestion, quality control, and standardized distribution pipeline to accomplish.

It should be able to take in observations from multiple transportation and weather-related sources without each one needing a completely custom treatment. The system should normalize the data into a common structure, run quality checks, and then publish it in a form that agencies, providers, and researchers can use reliably. Ideally, it would also flag bad or incomplete records instead of just passing them through, so downstream users can tell what is trustworthy.
It seems like you need normalization, quality checks, publication in a common format, and flagging of bad or incomplete records. Can you describe more about how the quality checks should work?

The quality checks should catch obvious errors like missing fields, out-of-range values, inconsistent timestamps, and conflicts between related measurements. I’d also expect some source-based checks, where we can treat certain feeds differently depending on their reliability or known issues. If something fails a check, it should be marked clearly so it can either be corrected, filtered out, or at least identified for users.
